clinicalPearls: A paraneoplastic hypoglycaemia caused by a solitary fibrous tumour (most often pleural, sometimes pelvic, retroperitoneal or meningeal) that secretes incompletely processed high-molecular-weight insulin-like growth factor 2, often termed big IGF-2.
The hypoglycaemia is fasting and hypoinsulinaemic: endogenous insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin are all suppressed, which sharply distinguishes it from insulinoma.
Big IGF-2 activates insulin and IGF-1 receptors, increasing peripheral glucose uptake and suppressing hepatic glucose output, growth hormone and IGF-1.
Characteristic biochemistry includes low insulin, low C-peptide, non-ketotic hypoglycaemia with low beta-hydroxybutyrate, suppressed growth hormone and IGF-1, and a raised IGF-2 to IGF-1 ratio.
Tumours are typically large and slow-growing, and neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, seizures) tend to occur with fasting, exertion or overnight.
Complete surgical resection is the definitive treatment and usually resolves the hypoglycaemia; recurrent hypoglycaemia may herald tumour recurrence.
In unresectable disease, glucocorticoids and sometimes growth hormone palliate hypoglycaemia, alongside continuous carbohydrate provision.
Solitary fibrous tumours characteristically harbour a NAB2-STAT6 gene fusion, and nuclear STAT6 immunostaining supports the histological diagnosis.
reference.pathophysiology: Solitary fibrous tumours are mesenchymal neoplasms, frequently pleural, defined by a NAB2-STAT6 fusion, and a subset secrete large amounts of incompletely processed pro-IGF-2 (big IGF-2). Because this high-molecular-weight form fails to assemble into the normal ternary complex with IGF-binding protein 3 and the acid-labile subunit, it instead circulates in smaller binary complexes that readily cross the capillary endothelium and remain biologically active. Big IGF-2 stimulates insulin receptors and IGF-1 receptors in muscle, fat and liver, increasing glucose uptake while suppressing hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, producing fasting hypoglycaemia. It also suppresses pituitary growth hormone secretion, lowering IGF-1 and thereby raising the IGF-2 to IGF-1 ratio; endogenous insulin, C-peptide and ketogenesis are all suppressed, yielding the characteristic non-ketotic, hypoinsulinaemic picture.
additionalDifferentials: Insulinoma with inappropriately raised insulin and C-peptide
Exogenous insulin or sulfonylurea use (iatrogenic or factitious)
Other IGF-2-secreting tumours (hepatocellular, mesothelioma, sarcoma, adrenocortical carcinoma)
Critical illness, sepsis, hepatic failure or severe malnutrition
additionalInvestigations: Timed sample during spontaneous hypoglycaemia for glucose, insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin and beta-hydroxybutyrate
IGF-2 and IGF-1 measurement with calculation of the IGF-2 to IGF-1 ratio
Growth hormone and cortisol response during hypoglycaemia
Sulfonylurea/meglitinide screen and insulin antibody testing
Cross-sectional imaging of chest and abdomen to localise a solitary fibrous tumour
Histology with nuclear STAT6 immunostaining and NAB2-STAT6 confirmation
Functional or whole-body imaging if the primary tumour remains occult
redFlags: Recurrent severe neuroglycopenia (seizures or loss of consciousness), especially nocturnal or on fasting
A rapidly enlarging thoracic or abdominal mass
Recurrence of hypoglycaemia after resection, suggesting tumour recurrence or malignant transformation
Respiratory compromise from a large pleural tumour
Evidence of metastatic or malignant solitary fibrous tumour
reference.prognosis: Complete resection of a benign solitary fibrous tumour usually cures the hypoglycaemia with an excellent outlook. Malignant, unresectable or recurrent tumours carry a worse prognosis and persistent hypoglycaemia.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing as insulinoma and pursuing pancreatic surgery, when insulin and C-peptide are actually suppressed.
Failing to calculate the IGF-2 to IGF-1 ratio, since routine assays may miss big IGF-2 and the absolute IGF-2 can appear normal.
Dismissing a known incidental pleural mass as unrelated to the hypoglycaemia.
Assuming benign behaviour, as these tumours can recur or metastasise years later.
Attributing hypoglycaemia solely to cachexia or malnutrition in a patient with cancer.

management: Doege-Potter syndrome is paraneoplastic hypoglycemia from a solitary fibrous tumor secreting big IGF-2; treatment targets the underlying tumor, not the hypoglycemia itself
For localized resectable disease, complete surgical resection is the primary and usually curative treatment and is expected to correct the hypoglycemia
If hypoglycemia persists after apparent complete resection, evaluate for residual or metastatic disease rather than treating it as an isolated endocrine problem

For locally advanced or borderline resectable tumors, assess feasibility of R0 resection and involve a multidisciplinary sarcoma team before deciding on neoadjuvant therapy or a change in surgical plan
For unresectable, metastatic, or recurrent disease, note that these tumors are resistant to standard anthracycline-based chemotherapy
Multi-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors directed against angiogenic pathways have the best-evidenced systemic activity in this histology
In the metastatic or unresectable setting, treatment goals are disease control and symptom or hypoglycemia palliation rather than cure
Surgery remains the mainstay whenever an R0 resection is achievable, including for isolated recurrences or resectable metastases
Radiotherapy is not established as a first line curative option and should be individualized by the sarcoma multidisciplinary team rather than used routinely
Tumor size greater than 10 cm and mitotic rate above 4 per 10 high power fields identify higher metastatic risk and should inform surveillance intensity
Retroperitoneal location carries a high risk of distant recurrence over a 10 year horizon, warranting long-term imaging follow-up even after complete resection
Fasting glucose and neuroglycopenic symptom monitoring can serve as an adjunct signal of tumor recurrence but should not replace structured oncologic surveillance imaging
Refer patients with a large SFT and unexplained hypoglycemia promptly to a sarcoma-experienced surgical oncology or multidisciplinary team for staging and resection planning

Refer unresectable, locally advanced, or metastatic disease to medical oncology for tyrosine-kinase-inhibitor-based systemic therapy, with endocrinology input for interim hypoglycemia management such as glucocorticoids and continuous carbohydrate provision
